1	Temperature-sensitive payloads such as medicines, diagnostic samples, and perishable foods are frequently distributed in insulated containers that carry their own thermal reserve. A container of this kind is loaded at a packing point, handed to one or more couriers, and opened at a destination that may be many hours away. Because the container travels unattended and often without electrical power, the thermal behaviour of the container has to be set at the moment of closing and cannot be corrected in transit.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate the use of such containers. The first is the distribution of cold within the payload space. A thermal reserve placed against one wall, or laid directly on top of a payload, cools the material nearest to it strongly and the material farthest from it weakly, so the payload experiences a spread of temperatures. Direct contact between the thermal reserve and the payload can drive the contacted items below the intended range while more distant items drift above it. Moving air distributes the effect of the reserve more evenly, but a fan, pump, or other powered air mover adds a battery, a failure mode, and a service burden, and is unwelcome in a container that has to be returned and used again.
4	
5	The second difficulty is that a container which relies on an internal air path only performs as intended if that path is actually present when the container is closed. Loose internal components are lifted, rotated, or nudged during loading and during transport. If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
6	
7	Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.
10

1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 6 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.
2	
3	## Overview of the carrier
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 2, and FIG. 5, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are of insulating construction, and the carrier can be returned for reuse.
6	
7	Referring also to FIG. 5, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.
8	
9	The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. The side supply passages 30 and the lower return passage 28 are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10.
10	
11	## The removable thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a rigid frame body. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.
14	
15	The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 at the centre of the rigid spacer frame 42 and facing the product region within the removable product tray 20, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.
16	
17	Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.
18	
19	## The registered passive circulation path
20	
21	The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.
22	
23	In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.
24	
25	The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
26	
27	## Lid-driven registration and retention
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.
30	
31	A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration before the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.
32

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 6 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.

## Overview of the carrier

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 2, and FIG. 5, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are of insulating construction, and the carrier can be returned for reuse.

Referring also to FIG. 5, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.

The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. The side supply passages 30 and the lower return passage 28 are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10.

## The removable thermal module

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a rigid frame body. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 at the centre of the rigid spacer frame 42 and facing the product region within the removable product tray 20, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.

Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.

## The registered passive circulation path

The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.

In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.

The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

## Lid-driven registration and retention

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration before the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.

Referring to FIG. 4, the same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. That pressing holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30.

Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Referring to FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items and are not to be opened. Withdrawing the removable absorbent wick 72 from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel 70 restores the carrier for the next journey.

## Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 6, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction, and the temperature-responsive latch 84 retains the indicator stem 82 against that action while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.

## Method of passively conditioning a payload

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 after that registration. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.

At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.

## Variations

The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent. The claims that follow define the invention, and each claim is to be read in the light of the whole of this description.

content.text: I have read all sources, draft sections, and figure briefs. Here is the review.

input.summary:
Ledger scope: I traced every claim limitation (claims 1–17), every numeral in draft/numerals.md (10–86), and every structure, relationship, result, position, connection and operating condition in draft/04-field.md through draft/10-abstract.md and figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-6.md to the USER disclosure (input/disclosure.md, mirrored in the single USER passage of input/conversation.md). input/brief.md was used only for formalities (title is a "working title" so the descriptive title is acceptable; "No priority claim" and "No federally sponsored research" match the "Not applicable." cross-reference and government-support sections). prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background makes no citation, so nothing needed prior-art tracing.

Supported and clean: the four bodies (shell 10 / tray 20 / module 40 / lid 60), tray feet 22 and lower return passage 28, tray side walls 24 spaced inward to form two side supply passages 30, perforations 26, rigid spacer frame 42 with two opposed cassettes 44, central inlet opening 46, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings 50 aligned with the side passages, the full passive flow sequence and "no fan, pump, or powered air mover", depending indexing rib 62 / mating channel 52 registration, gasket 64 sealing against upper edge 16 "after registration", resilient feet 54 on ledges 18, shallow condensate channel 70 with discharge openings 56 at duct lower ends, wick 72 and pull tab 74, and indicator 80/82/84/86 including irreversibility, manual reset and non-control of airflow. Method claims 12–17 map to the disclosed use and servicing sequence. Claims 4 and 5 (cassettes on opposite sides of the inlet; module lifting out as one piece with the tray thereafter) are entailed by "two opposed phase-change cassettes", "divides along faces of the cassettes", "central inlet", and "the spacer frame rests above the product tray", so I did not report them. Numeral integrity is sound: every numeral used appears once in the table with a single meaning, every table entry appears on at least one figure, and no figure carries a numeral absent from the table. Section line 2-2 uses the same designation in FIG-1 (repeated at both ends with arrows), FIG-2's caption, and draft/07-drawings.md; all four broken-circle callouts (central, right-hand upper, right-hand lower, left-hand) are designated identically in FIG-2, in each enlarged view's brief, and in the Brief Description. No drafting note, placeholder, open question or unresolved alternative remains in draft/ or figures/, and no "by way of example" or "any closed outline" shape hedge leaked into the application text — the schematic conventions stay inside the figure briefs.

Five findings, two critical. Both criticals are in figures/FIG-3.md, where the brief resolves an internal flow topology the inventor never disclosed. The disclosure says only that air "enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts". FIG-3 converts that into a specific route: each cassette "stops short of the upper web of the frame 42, leaving a blank open gap between its upper end and the underside of that web through which the space between the cassettes 44 communicates with the upper end of the duct 48 on that side", i.e. an over-the-top crossover from the inter-cassette space to the outboard ducts. FIG-3 also adds "a lower web portion of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 beneath each cassette 44 on each side of the opening 46", a flow boundary that forces that route. These are flow-path and contact-topology statements about a functional duct and port, so the "shown schematically" label does not excuse them; both must be removed and left unverbalized. Neither relationship appears anywhere in draft/08-detailed-description.md, so the figure would also depict structure the specification never describes.

The major finding is in figures/FIG-6.md: the indicator housing is specified as "closed at its outer end" with a hatched (solid) body, which contradicts the disclosed and claimed behaviour that the indicator is "visible from outside" and that the spring moves the stem "to a latched exposed position" (claim 9, claim 17, description ¶45–47). The outer-end closure is itself untraced; deleting it resolves both the contradiction and the fidelity gap without adding any structure.

Two minor findings: FIG-6 also states the spring's reaction surfaces and that it "is compressed", and places the latch "inside the housing" — an operating condition and relative locations the disclosure does not give (it says only that the stem is "retained by a temperature-responsive latch" and that "a spring moves the indicator stem"); and draft/10-abstract.md calls the shell an "insulated shell" where every other section, including claim 1, uses "insulated outer shell".

No other internal inconsistency was verified. The description's flow order ("passes through the perforations ... and returns through the lower return passage") reproduces the inventor's own wording verbatim and the figure briefs deliberately leave the perforation locations unspecified, so I did not treat that as a drafting defect; resolving it would require adding undisclosed structure. Advantage and problem-framing prose in the description (e.g. "the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box") mirrors the Background and follows from the disclosed registration relationship, so it is not reported as an untraced result.

findings.title: FIG-3 invents an over-the-top flow crossover from the inter-cassette space to the guide ducts
findings.detail: The brief specifies a particular internal flow route through the spacer frame: air reaches each downward guide duct 48 by passing over the top of the adjacent cassette 44 through a gap between the cassette's upper end and the underside of the frame's upper web. The disclosure describes only that air "enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts"; it never says how the space between the opposed cassettes communicates with the outboard ducts, never says a cassette stops short of any part of the frame, and never discloses an upper web closing the top of the inter-cassette space. This is a flow-path and flow-boundary relationship for a functional duct, so it is substantive notwithstanding the "schematic" framing, and it appears in no part of draft/08-detailed-description.md, meaning the figure would show a relationship the specification never describes.
findings.evidence: Candidate (figures/FIG-3.md): "Each cassette 44 stops short of the upper web of the frame 42, leaving a blank open gap between its upper end and the underside of that web through which the space between the cassettes 44 communicates with the upper end of the duct 48 on that side." Nearest source (input/disclosure.md ¶7): "Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages" — no affirmative passage anywhere in the disclosure or conversation discloses a gap above the cassettes, a cassette stopping short of the frame, or the route by which the inter-cassette space reaches the ducts.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, delete the sentence "Each cassette 44 stops short of the upper web of the frame 42, leaving a blank open gap between its upper end and the underside of that web through which the space between the cassettes 44 communicates with the upper end of the duct 48 on that side." and end the cassette bullet at "...each having an outboard surface facing the nearer outboard web." Retain the existing unnumbered bullet "The space between the two cassettes 44 is continuous with the opening 46 below it and communicates with both ducts 48, so that air entering the opening 46 passes along the opposed faces of the cassettes 44 and into the ducts 48.", which tracks the disclosed sequence without specifying an undisclosed crossover geometry.

findings.title: FIG-3 adds lower web portions closing the underside of the frame beneath each cassette
findings.where: figures/FIG-3.md, "Rigid spacer frame 42" bullet (line 6) and "Central inlet opening 46" bullet (line 7)
findings.detail: The brief specifies that the frame's underside is closed by lower web portions beneath each cassette on each side of the central inlet opening. That is a flow boundary: it prevents air from leaving the inter-cassette region downward except through the inlet, and together with the over-the-top gap it dictates the circulation route inside the module. The disclosure discloses only "a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes" with "a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings", and says nothing about the frame's web construction or which parts of its underside are closed. By contrast, the companion statement that the underside remains open at the lower end of each duct is traceable and should be kept.
findings.evidence: Candidate (figures/FIG-3.md): "a lower web portion of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 beneath each cassette 44 on each side of the opening 46, the underside of the frame 42 remaining open at the lower end of each duct 48"; and "drawn as an upper horizontal web, an outboard upright web at each side of the view, and short lower web portions, all continuous with one another". Nearest source (input/disclosure.md ¶7): "The thermal module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes... It includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings" — no affirmative passage discloses lower webs or a closed underside beneath the cassettes. The open lower end of each duct is supported by ¶11: "Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel."
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, delete ", and short lower web portions," from the frame bullet so it reads "drawn as an upper horizontal web and an outboard upright web at each side of the view, continuous with one another"; and in the central inlet bullet delete "a lower web portion of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 beneath each cassette 44 on each side of the opening 46," so the bullet reads "...opening downward out of the underside of the frame 42 and upward into the blank open space between the two cassettes 44, the underside of the frame 42 remaining open at the lower end of each duct 48."

findings.title: FIG-6 shows the indicator housing closed at its outer end, contradicting the disclosed exposed, externally visible indication
findings.where: figures/FIG-6.md, "Mechanical exposure indicator 80" bullet (line 6), read against draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶45–47 and draft/09-claims.md claims 9, 10 and 17
findings.detail: The brief draws the indicator as a solid hatched box "closed at its outer end" with the stem's outer end lying inside it. If the outer end of the housing is closed and hatched, outward movement of the stem cannot produce an indication visible from outside, so the depiction contradicts the description and the claims, which require the indicator to be "visible from outside" and the spring to move the stem "to a latched exposed position". The closed outer end is also itself untraced: the disclosure specifies no housing geometry at all. A schematic housing is an acceptable depiction convention, but stating that its outer end is closed adds an undisclosed feature that defeats the disclosed function.
findings.evidence: Candidate (figures/FIG-6.md): "Mechanical exposure indicator 80: a housing standing proud of the outer surface of the shell side wall 14, shown schematically as a hatched box of modest size, open toward the bore and closed at its outer end". Conflicting candidate text (draft/09-claims.md claim 9): "the insulated outer shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside... a spring that moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position". Source (input/disclosure.md ¶13): "The shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside... a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position." No source passage describes a housing or its outer end.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-6.md, delete "and closed at its outer end" so the bullet reads "Mechanical exposure indicator 80: a housing standing proud of the outer surface of the shell side wall 14, shown schematically as a hatched box of modest size, open toward the bore, its interior blank and aligned with the bore."

findings.title: FIG-6 specifies untraced latch placement, spring reaction surfaces and a compressed spring state
findings.where: figures/FIG-6.md, "Temperature-responsive latch 84" bullet (line 8), "Spring 86" bullet (line 9) and the closing unnumbered bullet (line 13)
findings.detail: The brief locates the latch inside the external housing, grounds the spring between a named internal surface of the indicator and a named face of the stem, and states as an operating condition that the spring is compressed. The disclosure says only that the stem is "retained by a temperature-responsive latch" and that "a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position". Relative location of a functional retaining element, the spring's reaction surfaces, and the compressed-versus-extended state are technical substance rather than page placement, and none is traceable. The spring's outward direction of action is traceable, because the exposed position is by definition outward and visible from outside, and latch-to-stem engagement is traceable from "retained by".
findings.evidence: Candidate (figures/FIG-6.md): "Temperature-responsive latch 84: a small body inside the housing, shown schematically as a short hatched block bearing against the stem 82..."; "Spring 86: a spring shown schematically as a series of connected loops in the interior of the housing, between an inward-facing internal surface of the indicator 80 and a face of the stem 82..."; "The spring 86 is compressed and acts on the stem 82 in the outward direction...". Nearest source (input/disclosure.md ¶13): "An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position." There is no affirmative passage on where the latch or spring sits or on the spring's state.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-6.md, change the latch bullet to "Temperature-responsive latch 84: a small body shown schematically as a short hatched block engaging the stem 82 so that the stem 82 is held against outward movement."; change the spring bullet to "Spring 86: a spring shown schematically as a series of connected loops acting on the stem 82 in the outward direction."; and change the closing bullet to "The spring 86 acts on the stem 82 in the outward direction, while the latch 84 holds the stem 82 against that movement."

findings.title: Abstract calls the shell an "insulated shell" while every other section uses "insulated outer shell"
findings.detail: The abstract names the first element "an insulated shell", whereas draft/06-summary.md, draft/08-detailed-description.md (element 10), draft/09-claims.md claim 1, and draft/numerals.md all use "insulated outer shell". Every numbered part must carry one designation across the application, and the abstract should use the same term as claim 1 for the same element.
findings.evidence: Candidate (draft/10-abstract.md): "A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid." Compare draft/09-claims.md claim 1: "an insulated outer shell having a shell floor, shell side walls rising from the shell floor, and an upper edge at a top of the shell side walls" and draft/numerals.md: "| 10 | insulated outer shell |".
findings.fix: In draft/10-abstract.md, replace "an insulated shell" with "an insulated outer shell". The abstract then runs 141 words, still within the 150-word limit of 37 CFR 1.72(b).

structured_output.summary:
Ledger scope: I traced every claim limitation (claims 1–17), every numeral in draft/numerals.md (10–86), and every structure, relationship, result, position, connection and operating condition in draft/04-field.md through draft/10-abstract.md and figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-6.md to the USER disclosure (input/disclosure.md, mirrored in the single USER passage of input/conversation.md). input/brief.md was used only for formalities (title is a "working title" so the descriptive title is acceptable; "No priority claim" and "No federally sponsored research" match the "Not applicable." cross-reference and government-support sections). prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background makes no citation, so nothing needed prior-art tracing.

Supported and clean: the four bodies (shell 10 / tray 20 / module 40 / lid 60), tray feet 22 and lower return passage 28, tray side walls 24 spaced inward to form two side supply passages 30, perforations 26, rigid spacer frame 42 with two opposed cassettes 44, central inlet opening 46, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings 50 aligned with the side passages, the full passive flow sequence and "no fan, pump, or powered air mover", depending indexing rib 62 / mating channel 52 registration, gasket 64 sealing against upper edge 16 "after registration", resilient feet 54 on ledges 18, shallow condensate channel 70 with discharge openings 56 at duct lower ends, wick 72 and pull tab 74, and indicator 80/82/84/86 including irreversibility, manual reset and non-control of airflow. Method claims 12–17 map to the disclosed use and servicing sequence. Claims 4 and 5 (cassettes on opposite sides of the inlet; module lifting out as one piece with the tray thereafter) are entailed by "two opposed phase-change cassettes", "divides along faces of the cassettes", "central inlet", and "the spacer frame rests above the product tray", so I did not report them. Numeral integrity is sound: every numeral used appears once in the table with a single meaning, every table entry appears on at least one figure, and no figure carries a numeral absent from the table. Section line 2-2 uses the same designation in FIG-1 (repeated at both ends with arrows), FIG-2's caption, and draft/07-drawings.md; all four broken-circle callouts (central, right-hand upper, right-hand lower, left-hand) are designated identically in FIG-2, in each enlarged view's brief, and in the Brief Description. No drafting note, placeholder, open question or unresolved alternative remains in draft/ or figures/, and no "by way of example" or "any closed outline" shape hedge leaked into the application text — the schematic conventions stay inside the figure briefs.

Five findings, two critical. Both criticals are in figures/FIG-3.md, where the brief resolves an internal flow topology the inventor never disclosed. The disclosure says only that air "enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts". FIG-3 converts that into a specific route: each cassette "stops short of the upper web of the frame 42, leaving a blank open gap between its upper end and the underside of that web through which the space between the cassettes 44 communicates with the upper end of the duct 48 on that side", i.e. an over-the-top crossover from the inter-cassette space to the outboard ducts. FIG-3 also adds "a lower web portion of the frame 42 closing the underside of the frame 42 beneath each cassette 44 on each side of the opening 46", a flow boundary that forces that route. These are flow-path and contact-topology statements about a functional duct and port, so the "shown schematically" label does not excuse them; both must be removed and left unverbalized. Neither relationship appears anywhere in draft/08-detailed-description.md, so the figure would also depict structure the specification never describes.

The major finding is in figures/FIG-6.md: the indicator housing is specified as "closed at its outer end" with a hatched (solid) body, which contradicts the disclosed and claimed behaviour that the indicator is "visible from outside" and that the spring moves the stem "to a latched exposed position" (claim 9, claim 17, description ¶45–47). The outer-end closure is itself untraced; deleting it resolves both the contradiction and the fidelity gap without adding any structure.

Two minor findings: FIG-6 also states the spring's reaction surfaces and that it "is compressed", and places the latch "inside the housing" — an operating condition and relative locations the disclosure does not give (it says only that the stem is "retained by a temperature-responsive latch" and that "a spring moves the indicator stem"); and draft/10-abstract.md calls the shell an "insulated shell" where every other section, including claim 1, uses "insulated outer shell".

No other internal inconsistency was verified. The description's flow order ("passes through the perforations ... and returns through the lower return passage") reproduces the inventor's own wording verbatim and the figure briefs deliberately leave the perforation locations unspecified, so I did not treat that as a drafting defect; resolving it would require adding undisclosed structure. Advantage and problem-framing prose in the description (e.g. "the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box") mirrors the Background and follows from the disclosed registration relationship, so it is not reported as an untraced result.

findings.title: FIG-3 invents an over-the-top flow crossover from the inter-cassette space to the guide ducts
findings.detail: The brief specifies a particular internal flow route through the spacer frame: air reaches each downward guide duct 48 by passing over the top of the adjacent cassette 44 through a gap between the cassette's upper end and the underside of the frame's upper web. The disclosure describes only that air "enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts"; it never says how the space between the opposed cassettes communicates with the outboard ducts, never says a cassette stops short of any part of the frame, and never discloses an upper web closing the top of the inter-cassette space. This is a flow-path and flow-boundary relationship for a functional duct, so it is substantive notwithstanding the "schematic" framing, and it appears in no part of draft/08-detailed-description.md, meaning the figure would show a relationship the specification never describes.
